title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance + ADR Index
author: Lena Ortiz
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document centralizes Redwood Inference's architecture and engineering standards across API, coding, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It pairs prescriptive guidance with an index of active ADRs to ensure consistent, auditable decisions for production-grade inference. Audience: Engineers, tech leads, security reviewers, and platform owners.

Summary of changes: Consolidates previously fragmented guidance into one canonical reference, clarifies SLOs and rollout steps for model-serving changes, and records key ADRs through 2026-Q1.

Contents (top-level)
1) API Standards
2) Coding Standards
3) Infrastructure & IaC Standards
4) Model-Serving Standards
5) Observability & Tracing Standards
6) Performance & SLOs
7) ADR index + Summaries
8) Governance, review process, and rollout checklist

1) API Standards

Intro: APIs are the contract between customers, internal services, and the runtime. Stability, backward compatibility, and predictable performance are primary goals.

Principles:
- Design for forward/backward compatibility: use semantic versioning for public endpoints (v1, v2), and maintain v1 for at least 12 months after v2 GA.
- Stable JSON over the wire. Prefer explicit fields to positional arrays for long-term compatibility.
- Keep response shapes small: avoid embedding full model metadata unless requested via ?expand=true.
- Use explicit error model with machine-readable codes.

Request/Response patterns:
- Use POST /v1/generate for text generation; accept input as {"prompt": "...", "instructions": "...", "metadata": {"customer_request_id": "..."}}
- Streaming: provide chunked transfer with application/json-seq and final status object {"status": "done", "tokens": N}.
- Pagination: cursor-based (next_cursor) for list endpoints.

Rate limiting & quotas:
- Per-API key RPS and concurrent request limits configurable in Console. Default hosted limits: 200 RPS API-key, 50 concurrent requests.
- Return HTTP 429 with body {"code":"rate_limited","retry_after": seconds}.

Security:
- All public endpoints require TLS 1.2+ and mTLS for Dedicated/Private control plane.
- Accept and forward tokens only over secure headers; never log bearer tokens.

API evolution checklist (pre-merge):
1. API owner documents backward compatibility assessment.
2. Add automated contract tests in CI (consumer-driven tests).
3. Update SDKs and per-route examples.
4. Notify customers via Console changelog and deprecation emails 60/30/7 days.

2) Coding Standards

Language priorities: Go (services & runtime), Python (evals, infra scripting), TypeScript (Console & SDKs), Rust (performance-critical components).

General rules:
- Single responsibility per package/module. Functions should be small and testable.
- Enforce formatting and linting: gofmt + golangci-lint for Go, black/ruff for Python, eslint + prettier for TypeScript. CI fails on lint errors.
- Strong typing: prefer explicit types over interface{} / any.
- Error handling: use structured errors with codes and context. Do not swallow errors silently.
- Tests: minimum 80% unit coverage for critical packages; 100% coverage expected for security-sensitive codepaths.

Repository layout guidance:
- monorepo for server-side services and infra modules; service boundaries enforced by top-level go/py/ts directories.
- Each service MUST include a README with ownership, run instructions, and SLOs.

Code review checklist (PR template):
- Description of change and user-visible impact.
- Performance considerations and benchmarks (if relevant).
- Security review: data access and logging changes.
- Migration/rollback steps and feature flags.

3) Infrastructure & IaC Standards

Infra primitives: Terraform for cloud provisioning, Kubernetes for orchestrating Dedicated/private clusters, and base AMI/VM images for on-prem packaging.

Standards:
- All Terraform code must live in modules and pass tflint + terraform validate in CI.
- State: use remote state with encryption (HashiCorp vault or cloud KMS).
- Network: default VPC segmentation pattern: control-plane (private), serving-plane (private subnets with egress NAT), public ingress (API gateway).
- Secrets: never store secrets in plaintext in Git. Use SOPS or Vault.

Capacity & scaling rules:
- GPU autoscaling policy: target utilization 70% sustained over 5 minutes to scale up; scale down when <40% for 10 minutes.
- Preemptible/Burst pools: can be used for non-SLA inference workloads only.

Change management:
- All infra changes require a Terraform plan posted to PR and one infra owner approval.
- Rollouts with stateful components must include migration plan and rollback playbook in PR description.

4) Model-Serving Standards

Goals: predictable latency, versioned models, safe fallbacks, and minimum regressions after rollouts.

Model artifact requirements:
- Standard model manifest (YAML) per model including: name, version, architecture, tokenizer, supported sequence lengths, KV-cache-friendly flag, quantization profile, and required GPU memory at 2048 context. Example manifest keys: name, version, arch, tokenizer, max_seq, kv_cache, quant_profile, mem_2048_mb.

Serving contracts:
- Model version pinning: Clients may pin to model@version; default is model@latest-stable.
- Backwards-compatible tokenizer changes are allowed; anything that changes tokenization must be a major version bump.
- Runtime MUST expose metrics: request_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99), tokens_generated, cache_hit_ratio, oom_count.

Batching and caching:
- Continuous batching is the default for throughput-oriented routes. Use per-route batching config with max_batch_size and max_queue_delay_ms.
- KV prefix caching enabled by default for interactive chat; policy to limit cached key sets per-tenant to avoid unbounded memory.

Quality & regression testing:
- Evaluation harness: every model release must pass the eval-harness (see /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness) with guardrails for task-specific benchmarks.
- Canary policy: 1% traffic for 24 hours, then 10% for 48 hours, then 100% if no regressions. Automated rollback on quality regression signals (see section 6).

Deployment checklist for model serving change:
1. Build model artifact and publish manifest.
2. Run full eval-harness and stability tests.
3. Deploy to canary pool; record metrics for 1 hour.
4. Increase canary per policy.
5. Full roll when monitoring and evals are green.

5) Observability & Tracing Standards

Goals: rapid detection of regressions, root cause analysis, and cost-aware retention.

Telemetry requirements per service:
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, error_rate (4xx/5xx breakdown), request_rate, tokens_per_second, cost_estimate_token_usd (for cost attribution).
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry spans per request with attributes: request_id, model_name, model_version, route, customer_id (hashed), latency_ms, kernel_selection. Traces must sample at 1% by default, 100% for errors and canary runs.
- Logs: structured JSON logs; sensitive fields redacted before ingestion.

Alerting thresholds (examples):
- High-latency: p95 request latency > 300ms for hosted text-generation routes for 5m => SEV-2 alert.
- Error spike: error_rate increase >3x baseline (15m window) or absolute >1% sustained for 10m => SEV-1 if impacting 5%+ customers.

Dashboards & ownership:
- Every service must publish a per-route dashboard (latency, traffic, errors, tokens, cache hit). Dashboards live in Grafana and link to runbooks.
- Ownership: on-call team owns alerts; service owner owns dashboards and SLOs.

6) Performance & SLOs

Global SLOs (hosted API default):
- Availability: 99.9% monthly for API control plane (excludes scheduled maintenance).
- Latency: p95 <= 300ms for small completion routes (<=128 tokens) and p95 <= 700ms for long-context routes (>1024 tokens).
- Error rate: <0.5% 5xx monthly.

Model-serving SLOs (per-model/per-route):
- p50/p95/p99 latency targets are declared in model manifest and enforced by runtime routing policies.
- Token throughput per-GPU baseline to be documented in model profile.

Performance testing guidance:
- Use benchmarking-and-perf-suite (eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite) to generate realistic workload distributions (prompt length, concurrency, seq length).
- Run load tests with production-like traffic patterns in a staging account and record p50/p95/p99 and GPU utilization.

Cost-aware controls:
- Autoscaling decisions should include cost-per-token estimates to avoid runaway scale when cost exceeds thresholds.
- Provide per-route token cost estimates to Console and allow product teams to set max_monthly_token_budget.

7) ADR index + Summaries (example decisions)

ADR-2024-06: Default model quantization strategy
- Decision: Use int8 dynamic quantization for CPU fallback and 4-bit quantization profiles (GPTQ-like) for GPUs where acceptable; maintain float16 for high-fidelity workloads.
- Rationale: Balance cost and quality; quant profiles evaluated in eval-harness.
- Owner: Research/Applied ML.

ADR-2025-01: API versioning strategy
- Decision: Semantic versioning for public endpoints; implement header-based negotiation for advanced features.
- Rationale: Minimize breakage across SDKs and integrations.
- Owner: Eng Developer Experience.

ADR-2025-07: Batching model for latency-sensitive routes
- Decision: Use adaptive continuous batching with per-route max_queue_delay_ms capped at 20ms for latency critical customer tiers.
- Rationale: Maintain low tail latency while preserving throughput.
- Owner: Eng Serving Runtime.

ADR-2026-02: Fallback routing and degradation ladder
- Decision: Implement multi-tier routing: primary (lowest-latency model), fallback-1 (quantized variant), fallback-2 (lower-cost regional model), and offline degrade to cached completion.
- Rationale: Improve availability and cost predictability.
- Owner: Platform & Runtime.

(Full ADR documents live under architecture-and-standards/adrs and are referenced in related_pages.)

8) Governance, review process, and rollout checklist

Standards governance:
- Standards steward: Architecture Guild (rotating 6-month term). All major changes require Architecture Guild sign-off.
- ADR lifecycle: Draft -> in_review (2 reviewers) -> published. ADRs older than 36 months require explicit re-review.

Rollout checklist for standards changes:
1. Create PR with updated standard and rationale.
2. Notify Architecture Guild and add at least two reviewers.
3. Run linters and CI; include compatibility tests where applicable.
4. Publish in-changelog and schedule a brown-bag for cross-team awareness.
5. Monitor relevant SLOs for 30 days post-rollout; trigger retrospective if regressions occur.

Appendices
A. Example model manifest (YAML)
---
name: redwood-gpt-large
version: 2026-01-15
arch: transformer
tokenizer: bpe
max_seq: 8192
kv_cache: true
quant_profile: q4_0
mem_2048_mb: "12288"
---

B. API error model example (JSON)
{
  "code": "invalid_input",
  "message": "Prompt exceeds max length (8192)",
  "request_id": "abcd-1234"
}

C. Quick CLI example: Deploy canary
# pipeline: deploy-model --manifest redwood-gpt-large-2026-01-15.yaml --target canary --percent 1
